primitives.name: StateStore
primitives.purpose: Key addressed durable key-value CRUD surface with optimistic concurrency tokens and optional TTL for language neutral state access.
primitives.api_signature:
from typing import Protocol, Any

class StateStore(Protocol):
    async def get(self, key: str) -> tuple[bytes, str | None]: ...
    async def save(self, key: str, value: bytes, etag: str | None = None, ttl_s: int | None = None) -> str: ...
    async def delete(self, key: str, etag: str | None = None) -> None: ...
    async def bulk_get(self, keys: list[str]) -> dict[str, tuple[bytes, str | None]]: ...
invariants: Save with a non None etag MUST reject when the stored etag differs and raise a conflict error.
Delete with a non None etag MUST NOT remove the entry when the etag no longer matches the stored version.
TTL expiry SHALL cause subsequent get calls to return a miss without invoking save or delete callbacks.
The returned etag on save MUST change whenever the stored value bytes change for a given key.
Bulk get MUST return a result for every requested key, using an absence marker for missing ones rather than omitting them.
Keys NEVER cross a tenant scope because store selection binds the scope at component configuration time.
primitives.extension_contract: Plug a new backend by implementing the StateStore protocol as a component adapter, register it under a name in the runtime component registry, and expose the same etag and TTL semantics; higher layers extend behavior by composing middleware around the protocol (encrypt on save, audit on delete).
primitives.consumption_example:
async def bump_counter(store: StateStore, key: str) -> int:
    raw, etag = await store.get(key)
    count = int(raw or b'0') + 1
    await store.save(key, str(count).encode(), etag=etag)
    return count

alternatives_considered: Exposing a raw Redis client per worker which leaks driver errors and skips ETag semantics
A thin repository per entity which pushes concurrency control into every tool instead of centralizing it

primitives.name: TransactionalBatch
primitives.purpose: Atomic multi key write unit that commits a set of upsert and delete operations to one state store under a single transaction boundary.
primitives.api_signature:
from typing import Protocol, Literal, Any
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class _Op:
    op: Literal['upsert', 'delete']
    key: str
    value: bytes | None
    etag: str | None

class TransactionalBatch(Protocol):
    def upsert(self, key: str, value: bytes, etag: str | None = None) -> 'TransactionalBatch': ...
    def delete(self, key: str, etag: str | None = None) -> 'TransactionalBatch': ...
    async def commit(self) -> None: ...
invariants: Commit MUST apply every queued operation atomically or apply none of them, with no partial visible state.
A conflicting etag on any queued operation MUST abort the entire batch and surface a conflict error.
After commit returns successfully the batch MUST NOT be reusable; reusing it SHALL raise a state error.
Operations inside one batch ALWAYS target the same state store instance to preserve the atomicity boundary.
Read operations are FORBIDDEN inside the batch because the contract covers only writes and deletes.
primitives.extension_contract: Backend authors extend the protocol by implementing an adapter for their store's native transaction API (Redis MULTI, Postgres BEGIN, Kafka transactions via transactional.id); composition happens at the runtime, which binds one adapter per configured store name.
primitives.consumption_example:
async def transfer(batch: TransactionalBatch, src: str, dst: str, amount: int) -> None:
    batch.upsert(src, str(-amount).encode()).upsert(dst, str(amount).encode())
    await batch.commit()

primitives.name: EventEnvelope
primitives.purpose: Canonical CloudEvents 1.0 shape that normalizes id, source, type, time and payload so downstream handlers parse the same structure regardless of transport.
primitives.api_signature:
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Any

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class EventEnvelope:
    id: str
    source: str
    type: str
    specversion: str = '1.0'
    datacontenttype: str | None = None
    dataschema: str | None = None
    subject: str | None = None
    time: str | None = None
    data: Any = None
    extensions: dict[str, str] | None = None
invariants: Producers MUST make the tuple (source, id) unique per distinct occurrence so consumers can deduplicate.
Resending the same logical event ALWAYS reuses the original id so retries do not appear as new occurrences.
specversion MUST equal '1.0' for envelopes produced under this contract.
Extension attribute names MUST follow the same naming rules as core attributes and CANNOT collide with reserved names.
time when present SHALL be an RFC 3339 timestamp in UTC with no timezone offset ambiguity.
primitives.extension_contract: Add custom attributes by registering an extension name in the extensions map following CloudEvents Extension Context Attributes rules; consumers extend by composing filters on type or subject via a decorator that wraps the handler.

AsyncAPI style schema registry coupling which pins transports earlier than needed

primitives.name: TopicBus
primitives.purpose: Publish and subscribe facade over a broker topic that delivers CloudEvents at least once to named subscriber groups with optional dead letter routing.
primitives.api_signature:
from typing import Protocol, Callable, Awaitable

Ack = Callable[[], Awaitable[None]]
Nack = Callable[[str], Awaitable[None]]

class TopicBus(Protocol):
    async def publish(self, topic: str, envelope: 'EventEnvelope') -> None: ...
    def subscribe(self, topic: str, group: str, handler: Callable[['EventEnvelope', Ack, Nack], Awaitable[None]]) -> None: ...
invariants: Delivery to a subscribed handler MUST be at least once by default, so handlers SHALL tolerate duplicates.
Inside one consumer group a given message ALWAYS goes to exactly one handler instance at a time.
Negative acknowledgement MUST cause redelivery or routing to a dead letter destination when configured.
Subscribers CANNOT rely on global ordering across topic partitions, only on partition local order.
Publish NEVER succeeds without the broker confirming the persisted append.
primitives.extension_contract: Swap brokers by implementing a TopicBus adapter per backend (Kafka, NATS JetStream, Redis Streams, RabbitMQ) and register it as a pubsub component; cross cutting behavior (retry, tracing, audit) plugs in as middleware wrapping the handler.

primitives.name: StreamSubject
primitives.purpose: Hierarchical dot separated event routing name that supports single token and trailing wildcard matching for consumer filters and stream captures.
invariants: Subject names MUST NOT contain null, whitespace, '.', '*' or '>' inside a token because these are the reserved separators.
The '>' wildcard SHALL appear only as the final token of a pattern and match one or more remaining tokens.
The '*' wildcard MUST match exactly one token, never zero and never multiple.
Names starting with '$' are FORBIDDEN for user subjects because that prefix is reserved for system use.
Publishers ALWAYS send to a fully specified subject; wildcards CANNOT appear in a publish call.
primitives.extension_contract: Extend routing by composing a StreamSubject with a predicate filter or by registering a subject mapping adapter on stream ingestion; custom taxonomies plug in by implementing a naming convention validator that wraps the constructor.
primitives.consumption_example:
def route(subjects: list[StreamSubject], pattern: str) -> list[StreamSubject]:
    return [s for s in subjects if s.matches(pattern)]

alternatives_considered: Plain string equality topics which lose the hierarchical fan out pattern
Regex based routing which is expressive but rejects NATS style constraints and costs more at scale

primitives.name: DeadLetterRoute
primitives.purpose: Named destination where undeliverable or repeatedly failed messages are routed after the redelivery budget is exhausted so they can be inspected or replayed.
invariants: A message delivered more than max_deliveries times MUST be routed to destination_topic and NEVER returned to the main topic.
The original EventEnvelope id and source ALWAYS survive routing so downstream audit can correlate.
max_deliveries MUST be a positive integer; zero or negative values SHALL raise a configuration error.
Routing to the dead letter destination CANNOT itself dead letter recursively in the same route.
The sink MUST record the terminal failure reason so operators can decide whether to replay.
primitives.extension_contract: Backends register a DeadLetterSink adapter per transport (Dapr deadLetterTopic, Kafka DLT, NATS dedicated stream) and the runtime composes it with the TopicBus; custom policies extend via a decorator that chooses different destinations based on failure type.
primitives.consumption_example:
async def park(sink, envelope: EventEnvelope, err: str) -> None:
    route = DeadLetterRoute(source_topic='orders', destination_topic='orders.dlq', max_deliveries=5)
    await sink.send(route, envelope, err, attempt=route.max_deliveries + 1)

primitives.name: PartitionLog
primitives.purpose: Ordered append only per partition event log identified by topic and partition number whose position is addressed by a monotonically increasing offset.
invariants: Offsets inside one PartitionLog MUST be strictly monotonically increasing for successfully appended records.
Reads at offset N ALWAYS return the same bytes for the lifetime of the log retention window.
A consumer group committed offset NEVER decreases except by an explicit reset operation initiated by an operator.
Cross partition ordering is FORBIDDEN as an assumption; only within one PartitionLog is order preserved.
When isolation is set to read_committed the reader CANNOT observe records from open or aborted transactions.
primitives.extension_contract: Adapters implement PartitionReader over a concrete broker client and plug into the ingestion pipeline; downstream processors extend by composing a projection handler that subscribes to a range of offsets via a decorator.
primitives.consumption_example:
async def tail(reader: PartitionReader, log: PartitionLog, group: str) -> list[int]:
    start = await reader.committed_offset(log, group)
    collected: list[int] = []
    async for off, _payload in reader.read_from(log, start):
        collected.append(off)
    return collected

primitives.name: WorkflowRun
primitives.purpose: Durable replayable orchestration identified by a workflow id that survives worker restarts and reconstructs state from a recorded event history.
primitives.api_signature:
from typing import Protocol, Any
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class WorkflowRun:
    workflow_id: str
    run_id: str
    task_queue: str

class WorkflowClient(Protocol):
    async def start(self, workflow_type: str, workflow_id: str, task_queue: str, args: tuple[Any, ...]) -> WorkflowRun: ...
    async def describe(self, workflow_id: str) -> WorkflowRun: ...
    async def cancel(self, workflow_id: str) -> None: ...
invariants: Workflow code MUST be deterministic so replay from the event history reconstructs the same decisions.
Non deterministic calls (random, wall clock time, direct network IO) are FORBIDDEN inside the workflow function.
A completed or canceled WorkflowRun CANNOT be resumed under the same run_id; reruns ALWAYS allocate a new run_id.
Every externally observable effect MUST flow through an activity, timer, signal or child workflow rather than direct side effects.
Starting a workflow with an id that already has an open run SHALL either reject or reuse according to the configured id reuse policy.
primitives.extension_contract: Register new workflow types as decorated functions on a worker polling a named task queue; extend behavior by composing interceptors on the worker that wrap workflow and activity invocations, and by implementing custom payload converters as adapters.
primitives.consumption_example:
async def kickoff(client: WorkflowClient) -> WorkflowRun:
    run: WorkflowRun = await client.start('ShipOrder', workflow_id='order-42', task_queue='orders', args=(42,))
    return run

primitives.name: ActivityCall
primitives.purpose: Workflow scoped unit of side effectful work scheduled with explicit timeouts and a retry policy that the runtime executes at least once on a worker.
primitives.api_signature:
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Protocol, Any

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class RetryPolicy:
    initial_interval_s: float
    backoff_coefficient: float
    maximum_attempts: int

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ActivityCall:
    name: str
    task_queue: str
    start_to_close_s: int
    schedule_to_close_s: int | None
    heartbeat_s: int | None
    retry: RetryPolicy
    args: tuple[Any, ...] = ()

class ActivityExecutor(Protocol):
    async def execute(self, call: ActivityCall) -> Any: ...
invariants: Execution semantics are at least once, so activity code MUST be idempotent under retry.
start_to_close_s MUST be set and be a positive integer; a missing value SHALL raise a configuration error.
Long running activities ALWAYS heartbeat within heartbeat_s; a missed heartbeat CANNOT be treated as success.
A failure whose attempt count reaches RetryPolicy.maximum_attempts MUST surface to the workflow as a terminal error.
Heartbeat details NEVER persist across a successful completion; they scope only to the in flight attempt and its retries.
primitives.extension_contract: Register activity implementations on a worker for a named task queue and extend cross cutting behavior with worker interceptors that wrap execute; adapters implement transport specific payload conversion.
primitives.consumption_example:
async def charge(executor: ActivityExecutor, order_id: int) -> str:
    call = ActivityCall(
        name='ChargeCard',
        task_queue='payments',
        start_to_close_s=30,
        schedule_to_close_s=120,
        heartbeat_s=10,
        retry=RetryPolicy(initial_interval_s=1.0, backoff_coefficient=2.0, maximum_attempts=5),
        args=(order_id,),
    )
    return await executor.execute(call)

primitives.why_essential: A common activity contract is the seam between deterministic orchestration and messy side effects; without it every tool invents its own retry loop and loses heartbeat progress on crash.
alternatives_considered: Bare retrying with tenacity which lacks timeouts scoped to schedule and heartbeat
A custom worker queue per feature which duplicates scheduling and observability plumbing

primitives.name: DurableTimer
primitives.purpose: Workflow scoped sleep that persists across worker outages and fires after a logical delay so long delays do not hold process resources.
invariants: A fired timer MUST be recorded as an event so workflow replay reconstructs the same fire point.
Wall clock sleep calls inside a workflow are FORBIDDEN because they break determinism and do not survive outages.
A canceled timer SHALL NEVER fire; cancellation ALWAYS reaches the workflow before a fired event is recorded.
delay_s MUST be non negative; a negative delay CANNOT be scheduled and raises an argument error.
A single worker NEVER caps the number of concurrent durable timers at the process level because timers persist server side.
primitives.extension_contract: Add scheduling backends by implementing TimerService as an adapter over the orchestrator, and compose cross cutting policies (quota, fairness) by wrapping start with middleware registered on the worker.
primitives.consumption_example:
async def park_until(svc: TimerService, wf_id: str, seconds: float) -> None:
    timer = DurableTimer(workflow_id=wf_id, timer_id=f'wait-{seconds}', delay_s=seconds)
    await svc.start(timer)

primitives.why_essential: Long waits without holding a thread, and deterministic replay of delays, are orchestrator level primitives; each tool rolling its own asyncio sleep loses persistence and replay correctness.
alternatives_considered: asyncio.sleep inside workflow code which disappears on process restart

primitives.name: WorkflowSignal
primitives.purpose: Asynchronous fire and forget write that delivers named input to an open workflow run and is recorded into the event history for replay.
invariants: A signal MUST be recorded as an event in the workflow history before it is considered delivered.
The sender CANNOT observe a return value from the signal; any response shape SHALL use an update or query instead.
Signals to a workflow that has closed MUST be rejected with a not found style error; signals NEVER start a closed run.
send_with_start ALWAYS atomically starts a new run or targets the existing open run under the same workflow id.
Handler code for a signal MUST follow the same determinism rules as the workflow itself.
primitives.extension_contract: Declare named signal handlers on the workflow type using a decorator; extend delivery semantics by composing worker interceptors that wrap the handler (for example, rate limiting or authorization).
primitives.consumption_example:
async def notify(sender: SignalSender, wf_id: str) -> None:
    sig = WorkflowSignal(workflow_id=wf_id, name='cancel_requested', payload={'reason': 'user'})
    await sender.send(sig)

alternatives_considered: Polling a state store from the workflow which wastes task slots and is not event driven
HTTP callbacks to the workflow worker which bypass the history and break replay

primitives.name: VirtualActor
primitives.purpose: Location transparent single writer object addressed by type and id that holds private state and processes one message at a time on activation.
invariants: Only one invocation of a given ActorId runs at a time; concurrent calls MUST queue in arrival order.
Actor state NEVER escapes the actor instance; callers ALWAYS read it through invoke, never via direct store access.
Reminders MUST survive actor deactivation and restart; they SHALL fire after the configured period regardless of host.
Timers within an actor CANNOT outlive deactivation; reminders are the durable option.
Caller code MUST NOT depend on the physical host of an actor because placement can migrate on failover.
primitives.extension_contract: Implement new actor behaviors by subclassing a base actor type and registering it with the runtime; cross cutting concerns (tracing, policy) plug in as server side interceptors around invoke.

sources.locator: docs.dapr.io/developing-applications/building-blocks/actors/actors-overview/ Turn based access, Placement, Timers vs Reminders sections

primitives.why_essential: Per entity serialization (single writer) is a common need for accounts, devices and sessions; centralizing the primitive prevents ad hoc locks sprinkled across tools that drift under load.
alternatives_considered: Row level locks in the database which do not scale horizontally and couple correctness to a single DB
Rebuilding actor semantics with consumer groups which lacks reminders and state affinity

primitives.name: DistributedLock
primitives.purpose: Named mutex with lease expiry that grants one holder exclusive access across processes and is released explicitly or by lease timeout on crash.
invariants: At most one caller MUST hold a given resource_id at a time; try_lock on a held lock returns None.
Locks ALWAYS auto release after lease_s elapses so a crashed holder CANNOT deadlock the resource forever.
Unlock with a non matching owner_id MUST be rejected so callers cannot release locks they do not own.
lease_s MUST be positive; a zero or negative lease SHALL raise a configuration error.
The primitive NEVER guarantees fairness across callers beyond the single holder invariant.
primitives.extension_contract: Swap backends by implementing DistributedLock as an adapter (Redis SET NX PX, etcd lease, Consul session) and register it as a component; higher guarantees (fencing tokens) plug in by wrapping try_lock in a middleware that annotates the handle.
primitives.consumption_example:
async def with_critical_section(lock: DistributedLock, resource: str, owner: str) -> bool:
    handle = await lock.try_lock(resource, owner, lease_s=30)
    if handle is None:
        return False
    try:
        return True
    finally:
        await lock.unlock(handle)

primitives.why_essential: Coordinating rare sequential work across workers (backfills, leader only cron) needs one contract; scattering ad hoc Redis SETNX code loses lease semantics and owner checks.
alternatives_considered: Advisory Postgres locks which tie correctness to one database and one transaction

primitives.name: KeyValueBucket
primitives.purpose: Named bucket of key value entries with optimistic create and update and a watch channel for change notifications derived from an underlying stream.
primitives.api_signature:
from typing import Protocol, AsyncIterator
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class KvEntry:
    key: str
    value: bytes
    revision: int

class KeyValueBucket(Protocol):
    async def create(self, key: str, value: bytes) -> KvEntry: ...
    async def update(self, key: str, value: bytes, revision: int) -> KvEntry: ...
    async def get(self, key: str) -> KvEntry | None: ...
    async def delete(self, key: str, revision: int | None = None) -> None: ...
    def watch(self, key: str) -> AsyncIterator[KvEntry]: ...
invariants: create MUST fail when the key already exists; it NEVER overwrites a present value.
update MUST fail when the supplied revision does not match the stored revision (compare and swap semantics).
Every successful write ALWAYS increases the entry revision monotonically.
Watch channels SHALL emit changes in revision order for a given key and CANNOT skip a revision without a gap signal.
Deleting a key NEVER frees its historical revisions if history retention is configured greater than one.
primitives.extension_contract: Backends implement KeyValueBucket as an adapter over JetStream, etcd or equivalent compare and swap store and register per bucket name; watchers extend via a decorator that composes filters on key prefix or revision range.
primitives.consumption_example:
async def ensure_feature(kv: KeyValueBucket, name: str) -> bytes:
    existing = await kv.get(name)
    if existing is not None:
        return existing.value
    entry = await kv.create(name, b'off')
    return entry.value

sources.locator: docs.nats.io/nats-concepts/jetstream Key Value Store section: create, update, watch, revisions

primitives.why_essential: Feature flags, session tokens and config blobs need compare and swap plus change notifications; a shared bucket contract prevents every tool from rebuilding optimistic update on top of a raw cache.
alternatives_considered: Plain string cache with TTL only which lacks compare and swap and change notification
Full relational row with triggers which is far heavier than the access pattern needs

primitives.name: RpcInterceptor
primitives.purpose: Per call middleware that wraps a remote procedure invocation to read or mutate metadata, enforce deadlines and translate errors consistently across services.
invariants: Interceptors MUST call next exactly once per invocation unless they deliberately short circuit with a status.
Metadata keys that end with '-bin' ALWAYS carry binary values and CANNOT be compared as plain strings.
Keys starting with 'grpc-' are FORBIDDEN for user metadata because that prefix is reserved by the runtime.
A deadline propagated in ctx MUST NOT be extended by an interceptor; it SHALL only be shortened or respected.
Cancellation signals NEVER cross interceptor boundaries silently; every interceptor SHALL honor cancel or raise a cancellation error.
primitives.extension_contract: Plug an interceptor into the chain by registering it on the client or server channel at construction time; compose multiple interceptors as an ordered list where earlier entries sit closer to the network and later entries closer to the handler.

sources.locator: grpc.io/docs/what-is-grpc/core-concepts/ Metadata and Deadlines/Timeouts paragraphs
grpc.io/docs/guides/interceptors/ When to use, Client vs Server, Interceptor ordering sections

primitives.why_essential: Authentication, tracing, rate limiting and deadline discipline must apply uniformly to every RPC; an interceptor contract is where those concerns compose without editing each generated stub.
alternatives_considered: Decorators on each service method which duplicate logic per endpoint
Global monkey patching of the RPC client which breaks generated stubs on upgrade

primitives.name: OutboundBinding
primitives.purpose: Declarative adapter that lets the application invoke an external resource through a named operation and metadata without embedding the vendor SDK.
invariants: The operation field MUST be one of the operations declared by the binding component; unknown values SHALL be rejected.
binding_name ALWAYS refers to a component already registered in the runtime; an unresolved name CANNOT invoke anything.
Metadata keys NEVER include secrets in plaintext because binding metadata can be logged by observability layers.
Binary payloads MUST round trip unchanged; the adapter CANNOT mutate data bytes implicitly.
Invocation timeouts SHALL be honored by the adapter or explicitly surfaced as a deadline error.
primitives.extension_contract: Add a new external system by implementing the OutboundBinding adapter (HTTP, S3, SMTP, SendGrid) and declaring it as a component with supported operations; applications extend by composing decorators around invoke for retry or circuit breaking.
primitives.consumption_example:
async def email(binding: OutboundBinding, to: str, body: bytes) -> None:
    inv = BindingInvocation(
        binding_name='sendgrid',
        operation='create',
        data=body,
        metadata={'emailTo': to},
    )
    await binding.invoke(inv)

sources.locator: docs.dapr.io/developing-applications/building-blocks/bindings/bindings-overview/ Output bindings, operation field, metadata sections

primitives.why_essential: Keeping every external integration behind one declarative adapter protects the skill from SDK churn and makes capabilities addressable by name; tools reference bindings instead of vendor packages.
alternatives_considered: Direct vendor SDK calls inside each tool which couples deployments and credentials management
HTTP only facade which loses operation taxonomy and typed metadata

cross_cutting_insights: Every durable transport in the catalog (Kafka, NATS JetStream, Dapr pub/sub) ships at-least-once by default, pushing idempotency and dedup keys into the application contract rather than the broker.
Identity tuples recur across sources: (source, id) in CloudEvents, (topic, partition, offset) in Kafka, (workflow_id, run_id) in Temporal, (actor_type, key) in Dapr actors - one shape per concern.

Optimistic concurrency is the shared write gate: ETags in Dapr state, revisions in NATS KV, sequence numbers in Kafka idempotent producer, and maximum_attempts in Temporal retry policies all reject stale writes.

Component and interceptor chains are the universal extension seam - Dapr component adapters, gRPC interceptors, Temporal worker interceptors and Kafka consumer interceptors all compose around a core primitive.

Determinism boundaries mark the orchestration primitives: Temporal workflows forbid direct IO and wall clock, funneling all side effects through activities, timers and signals recorded in an event history.
Dead letter and retry topology is explicit in every durable broker: Dapr deadLetterTopic, Kafka retry topics, NATS max deliveries - tools that ignore this reinvent parking lots per feature.
Placement transparency appears in Dapr virtual actors and Temporal task queues: callers address logical ids and the runtime chooses the host, which is why tools MUST NOT cache host identity.
gaps_observed: SKILL-001 lacks a durable workflow primitive; long running orchestration is still modeled as chained background jobs without event history.
No CloudEvents envelope shape is enforced on the existing event bus, so (source, id) dedup is not guaranteed across producers.
Virtual actor style single writer entities are missing; hot keys fall back to row locks or in process asyncio locks.
Distributed lock primitive with lease expiry is not exposed; tools reuse cache TTL tricks that drift under clock skew.
Dead letter route configuration is ad hoc per tool and not a first class primitive tied to the TopicBus contract.
No key value bucket with compare and swap plus watch; feature flag and session stores rely on plain cache semantics.
